title: Интровертная многоножка
description: Интровертная многоножка.
sourceDescription: Introverted Millipede. Earth had been conquered 350 million years ago by the representatives of the arthropods, among which were the millipedes (Diplopoda) depicted on the picture. These ground-dwelling animals have a lot of segments with two pairs of legs on them. The animal on the left side is a member of a species of Julus , its body is composed of hard, interlocking, sliding parts. The other one on the right side is a member of a species of Polydesmus ; it has a pair of defensive glands on each segment on its back. The photograph was taken by the scanning electron microscope Hitachi S-4700 with 70 times magnification and has been colored in Adobe Photoshop.

sourceDescription: In summer, some polar bears do not make the transition from their winter residence on the Svalbard islands to the dense drift ice and pack ice of the high arctic where they would find a plethora of prey. This is due to global climate change which causes the ice around the islands to melt much earlier than previously. The bears need to adapt from their proper food to a diet of detritus, small animals, bird eggs and carcasses of marine animals. Very often they suffer starvation and are doomed to die. The number of these starving animals is sadly increasing.

Built in 1872, it was the first building in the world with a visible metallic structure and is also characterized by its ceramic tiles patterns. The three years above the entrance correspond respectively to the year the old mill was built (1157), the year the Menier factory was moved to Noisiel (1825) and to the year the Saulnier Mill replaced the old one. The Menier chocolate factory is now headquarters of Nestlé France. This picture is a mosaic of 6 photos (2x3) taken with a Canon EOS 400D+EF 100mm f/2.8 Macro at 100mm, f/8.0, 1/800 sec and ISO 200. sourceDescription: Liudgerhaus (left), Diözesanbibliothek (right), Überwasserkirche (background) in Münster , North Rhine-Westphalia , Germany The Liudgerhaus in Münster is the central education and conference center of the Diocese of Münster. It was built in the first half of the 20th century and named after Saint Liudger, the first bishop of Münster († 809). To this day, the building serves as a place for church education, training, and meetings. The Liudgerhaus is closely linked to the Diocesan Library of Münster, one of Germany’s most important specialized theological libraries. Its origins date back to the time of the diocese; it preserves an extensive collection of theological literature, historical prints, and church documents. Parts of the facilities were damaged during World War II , but were later rebuilt and modernized. Today, the building complex combines tradition with contemporary educational work. It is an important place for ecclesiastical scholarship, pastoral training, and cultural remembrance in the diocese of Münster.

sourceDescription: Night view of Berlin Hauptbahnhof (English: Berlin Central Station ), main railway station in Berlin , Germany . The station came into full operation in May 2006 and is located on the site of the historic Lehrter Bahnhof , which was opened in 1871 as the terminus of the railway linking Berlin with Lehrte (location near Hanover ), which later became Germany's most important east-west main line. Following heavy damage during World War II , limited services to the main station were resumed, but then suspended in 1951. In 1957, with the railways to West Berlin under the control of East Germany , Lehrter Bahnhof was demolished, but Lehrter Stadtbahnhof continued as a stop on the S-Bahn. In 1987, it was extensively renovated to commemorate Berlin's 750th anniversary, and again in 2006 to its current appearance.

sourceDescription: Lüdinghausen Castle, Lüdinghausen, North Rhine-Westphalia , Germany Lüdinghausen Castle is located in the center of Lüdinghausen and is a typical Münsterland moated castle. Its origins date back to the 13th century. It was probably built by the Lords of Lüdinghausen as a fortified noble residence. The castle was surrounded by wide moats and consisted of an outer bailey and a main castle. Over the centuries, it changed hands several times and was expanded and redesigned. After military use, it lost its importance in the 18th and 19th centuries. Today, the complex has been restored and is used for cultural purposes. It houses event rooms and serves as a venue for exhibitions, concerts, and celebrations. Together with the nearby Vischering Castle , it shapes the townscape and underlines Lüdinghausen’s reputation as the “town of three castles”.

sourceDescription: Illuminated window of the Observant Church in Münster , North Rhine-Westphalia , Germany The Observant Church in Münster was built in the 17th century as a monastery church for the Franciscan Observants. The order was a reform movement within the Franciscans and placed particular emphasis on poverty and preaching. Construction of the church began in 1601, and it was built in the simple architectural style of the order. It was part of a monastery complex near what is now the city center. During secularization at the beginning of the 19th century, the monastery was dissolved and the buildings were used for other purposes. The church suffered severe damage during the Second World War. After reconstruction, it was integrated into the urban development in a modified form. Only parts of the original complex remain. The Observant Church is a reminder of Münster’s long monastic tradition and the importance of the mendicant orders for the religious life of the city.

sourceDescription: Art installation “Himmelsleiter” (Billi Thanner, 2022/23) at the tower of the St Lamberti Church in Münster , North Rhine-Westphalia , Germany The “Himmelsleiter” (Ladder to Heaven) by Viennese artist Billi Thanner, which was previously on display at St. Stephen’s Cathedral , was installed on and in St. Lambert’s Church on September 3, 2022. The outer part will light up for the last time in Münster on March 2, 2024 and will then leave the church after several extensions to be installed on the church of Saint Eustache in Paris from May 2024. The inner part will remain in Münster. The art installation consists of two parts. A 36-meter-long section is mounted on the outside of the tower of St. Lambert’s Church and a 12-meter-long section on the inside.

sourceDescription: Southwest portal with Tree of Jesse of St Lamberti Church in Münster , North Rhine-Westphalia , Germany St. Lamberti is a Roman Catholic parish church in Münster’s old town . It was built between 1375 and 1525 as a market and civic church and is located on Lambertikirchplatz and at the corner of Salzstraße and Prinzipalmarkt . St. Lamberti is the most important sacred building of the Westphalian late Gothic period. It is named after St. Lambert of Liège. A special feature are three iron baskets attached to the tower, in which the bodies of the three leaders of the Anabaptist kingdom of Münster, Jan van Leiden , Bernd Krechting, and Bernd Knipperdolling, were displayed in 1536 after they had been publicly tortured and executed in the square in front of the church. From 9 p. m. to midnight, a tower watchman or watchwoman blows a horn every half hour. The office has existed since 1379.

sourceDescription: Tormin Bridge (at sunrise), Münster , North Rhine-Westphalia , Germany The 145-meter-long Tormin Bridge is a pedestrian and bicycle bridge in Münster. It spans the Aasee lake and connects parts of the city center with adjacent residential and green areas. It was built in the 20th century as part of urban transport and road planning. The aim was to create safe crossings for pedestrians and, in particular, for cyclists, who are very numerous in Münster. The bridge has a functional design and blends inconspicuously into the cityscape. The design is by architects Fritz König and Albert Thomas. It was named after Richard Tormin, an engineer and city planning officer. He was also responsible for the previous structure, built in 1926. The current bridge was inaugurated on May 27, 1989.

sourceDescription: Elizabeth Quay Bridge, Perth , Western Australia , Australia The Elizabeth Quay Bridge is a striking pedestrian bridge in Perth city center. It was built as part of the Elizabeth Quay urban development project, which aimed to strengthen the connection between the city center and the Swan River. The bridge opened in 2016. Its curved, asymmetrical design is characteristic. Two sloping steel arches support the structure and give it a dynamic, modern shape. With a length of around 110 meters, it spans a side arm of the Swan River and connects the promenade with the island in the harbour basin. The bridge is intended exclusively for pedestrians and cyclists and offers views of the Perth skyline . In the evening, it is illuminated and is a popular photo motif. The Elizabeth Quay Bridge symbolizes the urban renewal of the waterfront area and the opening of the city to the water.

sourceDescription: Cheetah hissing after a meal in Kalahari Desert, Namibia. Cheetahs hiss primarily as a defensive warning. Unlike larger big cats that rely on strength, cheetahs are relatively lightweight and avoid direct conflict whenever possible. Hissing helps them appear more threatening and signals to potential predators or rivals (such as lions or hyenas) to keep their distance. This behavior is especially common when a cheetah feels cornered, is protecting its cubs, or is guarding a kill. In this photography the cheetah was hissing to protect its meal.

sourceDescription: In summer, some polar bears do not make the transition from their winter residence on the Svalbard islands to the dense drift ice and pack ice of the high arctic where they would find a plethora of prey. This is due to global climate change which causes the ice around the islands to melt much earlier than previously. The bears need to adapt from their proper food to a diet of detritus, small animals, bird eggs and carcasses of marine animals. Very often they suffer starvation and are doomed to die. The number of these starving animals is sadly increasing.

sourceDescription: Desert-adapted elephant dust bathing in Damaraland, Namibia. Desert-adapted elephants often dust-bathe by spraying sand or dust over their bodies with their trunks. This behavior helps protect their skin from intense sun and heat, acts as a natural insect repellent, and creates a protective layer that reduces moisture loss in the harsh desert environment. Desert-adapted elephants are the same species than African bush elephants ( Loxodonta africana ) but have behavior and physical adaptations for life in extreme desert environments. They are generally slimmer and slightly smaller than typical bush elephants and weighing toward the lower end of the species’ range due to limited food availability. Although African bush elephants can live 60–70 years in the wild, desert-living populations often have shorter average lifespans (40-50 years) because of the harsh conditions they live in.

sourceDescription: Baird's tapir mother and juvenile, Alajuela Province, Costa Rica. This is an endangered species, with only 3,000 - 5,000 left in the world. Famously secretive and primarily nocturnal, so this was a lucky moment. We went on a hike and found most of the park closed due to flooding. We explored where we could, seeing almost nothing outside of wet plants (and a famously bright blue river, Rio Celeste, which was brown that day). Just when we were hiking back out, we saw these tapirs foraging in the distance. Apparently sometimes on especially rainy days they're seen during daytime hours. After a short while of standing still and watching these two, they decided to cross the path right in front of us! For the rest of the trip, we'd mention this experience to locals/guides, and none had ever seen a baby in the wild before (and adults only a handful of times). Extraordinarily lucky, memorable experience.

sourceDescription: Dülmen ponies in the Wildbahn in the Merfelder Bruch (COE-004) in the morning fog at sunrise, Merfeld, Dülmen , North Rhine-Westphalia , Germany The Dülmen horse is a breed of pony that lives mainly in Dülmen in Westphalia in the Merfelder Bruch. Around 300 to 400 horses live in this fenced-off area, also known as the Wild Horse Trail, largely unaffected by humans. The wild horses of Dülmen were first mentioned in documents in 1316. One of the oldest German horse breeds, originally called Dülmener Brücher, these horses have been listed on the Red List of endangered livestock breeds by the Society for the Preservation of Old and Endangered Domestic Animal Breeds since February 1994. From a biological point of view, the Dülmen horse is not a wild horse. The name refers to its semi-wild lifestyle.

sourceDescription: Dead camel thorn tree ( Vachellia erioloba ) in Deadvlei , Namibia. The trees in Deadvlei grew approximately 900 years ago when periodic flooding of the Tsauchab River created a fertile marsh, but they died between 600 and 700 years ago after encroaching sand dunes obstructed the water flow. Due to the extreme aridity and lack of moisture in the Namib Desert, the wood has not decomposed; instead, the remains have been preserved and blackened by centuries of intense solar radiation.

title: Кристально чистое небо в любую ночь – это всегда радость
description: Кристально чистое небо в любую ночь – это всегда радость.
sourceDescription: A crystal-clear sky on any night is always a joy to behold. But if you are on the Chajnantor Plateau, at 5000 metres altitude in the Chilean Andes and one of the best places in the world for astronomical observations, it could be an experience that you’ll remember for your whole life. This panoramic view of Chajnantor shows the antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) against a breathtaking starry night sky. In the foreground, we can see some of ALMA’s antennas, working together. The plateau appears curved, because of the effect of the wide-angle lens used. ALMA is the world’s most powerful telescope for studying the Universe at submillimetre and millimetre wavelengths. Construction work for ALMA will be completed in 2013, and a total of 66 of these high-precision antennas will be operating on the site. At the moment, the telescope is in its initial phase of Early Science Observations. Even though it is not fully constructed, the telescope is already producing outstanding results, outperforming all other submillimetre arrays. In the sky above the antennas, countless stars shine like distant jewels. Two other familiar celestial objects also stand out. First, the image is crowned by the Moon. Second, outshone by the glow of the Moon, it is possible to distinguish the Milky Way as a hazy stripe across the sky. Dark regions within the band are areas where the light from background stars is blocked by interstellar dust. This photograph was taken by ESO Photo Ambassador , Babak Tafreshi . Babak is founder and leader of The World At Night, an international project to produce and exhibit a collection of stunning photographs and time-lapse videos of the world’s landmarks with a backdrop of the most beautiful celestial wonders. ALMA, an international astronomy facility, is a partnership of Europe, North America and East Asia in cooperation with the Republic of Chile. ALMA construction and operations are led on behalf of Europe by ESO, on behalf of North America by the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO), and on behalf of East Asia by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (NAOJ). The Joint ALMA Observatory (JAO) provides the unified leadership and management of the construction, commissioning and operation of ALMA.

sourceDescription: This striking low-angle shot captures the neoclassical majesty of Ancona’s War Memorial, designed by Guido Cirilli and inaugurated in 1932. THE INSCRIPTION - The photo highlights Giacomo Leopardi's touching dedication, " Voi ch'offriste il petto " ( You who offered your chest ), honoring those who fell during World War I. THE MATERIAL - The structure is built from Istrian stone, a durable limestone from across the Adriatic known for its brilliant white sheen and resistance to the salty sea air. HISTORICAL FACT - To satisfy the regime without compromising his vision, Cirilli tucked the required fasces into a graceful floral pattern. This subtle placement kept the iconography in the background, preserving the purity of the monument’s original meaning. COMPOSITION - The perspective emphasizes the austerity of the Doric order, contrasting the ivory stone against the deep blue sky to evoke a sense of timelessness and solemnity.

sourceDescription: The Best Farm/ L’Hermitage Slave Village site , Monocacy National Battlefield , Frederick, Maryland, USA, in early morning shadows. The house is an unusual example of a mixture of the local Federal style and Caribbean French Colonial styles of building and plantation culture, transplanted from Haiti / Saint-Domingue to central Maryland. It was built as the home of the Vincendrière family, who fled Saint-Domingue during the Haitian Revolution , and came to Maryland to establish a version of the plantation culture with which they were familiar. L'Hermitage was one of the largest slave-holding plantations in Maryland, and was notable for its brutal treatment of those enslaved there. The adjacent lands are documented as L'Hermitage Slave Village Archeological Site . The lands were fought over during the Battle of Monocacy in 1864 during the American Civil War. The hip-roofed barn, unusual for Maryland, is seen to the rear. Enoch Louis Lowe , 29th Governor of Maryland, was born at L'Hermitage in 1820, son of Bradley Samuel Adams Lowe and Adelaide Bellumeau de la Vincendrière

sourceDescription: Colorful houses in Wale Street , Cape Town , Western Cape , South Africa Bo-Kaap is a historic neighborhood above the center of Cape Town. It was established in the 18th century when the Dutch colonial administration built houses for enslaved people from Southeast Asia, India, and East Africa. Many of them were Muslims and later became known as “Cape Malays”. After their liberation in the 19th century, Bo-Kaap developed into a center of Islamic culture in the Cape. Mosques such as the Auwal Mosque from 1794 bear witness to this tradition. The colourfully painted houses, originally an expression of newly won freedom, now characterise the image of the neighbourhood. Despite gentrification, Bo-Kaap remains an important symbol of cultural heritage and resilience in South Africa.

sourceDescription: The Charnel House, located in a corner of the graveyard at St Helen's Church in Cliffe, Kent, England. The Charnel House was built during the mid 19th century. It was used as a make-shift mortuary until the bodies were taken away to be buried. Its location close to the river Thames is key as bodies found were washed up or floating along the Thames were retrieved and taken to the charnel house to be stored awaiting identification and burial. The building continued to be used until the start of the twentieth century, when a series of Public Health Acts forced buildings such as this to become redundant. After this, the Church used it for storage and at one time a hive of bees was also put in there to deter intruders. It is now classified as a Grade II listed building by English Heritage.
